newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Analysts sceptical about CA sale.
newsitem.headline: Analysts sceptical about CA sale.

text.p: Austria heaved a sigh of relief on Sunday after the government struck a long-awaited deal on the sale of the country's most prestigious bank Creditanstalt, but analysts were sceptical about the last-minute breakthrough.

"It has solved the problem of getting the government some money but it's opened up a whole new can of worms in terms of what they can make of it and I'm sceptical they can make very much," said Victoria Maxwell, analyst at James Capel in London.

"Whether they can do what's required to build a competitive bank in Europe is debatable," she added. "The general inefficiency within the Austrian banking system makes me very dubious about whether they can actually get the synergy gains and efficiency gains they need."

Bank Austria 's 17.2 billion schilling ($1.55 billion) offer won the bid, ending a seven-year-long battle over the privatisation of the government's 70 percent stake in Austria's flagship bank and averting a potential government collapse.

The dominant Social Democrats and conservative coalition partner People's Party had been at loggerheads over the sale, with the latter determined to prevent the sale of the establishment bank to "socialist" Bank Austria.
The conservatives eventually conceded the sale in return for a guarantee that Bank Austria would be taken out of public control and Creditanstalt remain independent for five years.

"I still have my doubts that in the long run the conservatives are really satisfied with the decision. Maybe tomorrow they will wake up and say "Oh my God what have we done'," said Alfred Reisenberger at IMI Group Sigeco.
He saw the fact that Creditanstalt would not be privatised immediately as unfavourable for Austria's banking sector.

"Creditanstalt has been sacrificed to bring the budget deficit down to meet the Maastricht criteria, which means the overdue alignment of the banking scene has been artificially delayed by such a decision," he said.
"There might be a shakeup but as Creditanstalt will remain an independent bank for the next five years this is an indication that nothing will change (in that time)," he added.
Analysts agreed there remained strong doubts about Bank Austria's ability to digest Creditanstalt effectively.

"The political concessions make the deal for Bank Austria less attractive, but I'm pleased the government coalition stayed intact," said Roland Neuwirth, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Vienna.
The linkup of Austria's two top banks will create a financial powerhouse with some 1,300 billion schillings in total assets, employing more than 16,000 people.

"It's going to make it more difficult for banks like Raiffeisen, which will now be tiny in comparison," said James Capel's Maxwell. "I wouldn't be surprised if we see further consolidation among the smaller banks."

Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa on Sunday predicted synergies from the merger would help the new banking group double its earnings per share within the next five years. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
